RISC-V ISA documentation - A modern well-documented instruction set without legacy stuff

The ISA documentation is really well written and quite readable even if you have little experience with assembly. What's quite interesting is how few instructions are actually needed. Just be aware that in actual RISC-V assembly there are quite a number of pseudo-instructions which expand to actual instructions, for example j (jump) is an alias for jalr (jump and put the address of the instruction following the jalr in a register, i.e. jump and keep track of where to return to) with destination register 0 (writing to register 0 is a noop). Unfortunately I've never found a good listing of those instructions which are used in the actual .S files.

When I was a kid, it was "dressing up", or "fancy dress". When did it become "cosplay" and what's the difference?

Well, cosplay is usually reserved for anime or video games, though it has been applicable to more westernized stuff like cartoons or television in recent years.

Edit: And it's usually a lot higher quality than just dressing up for Halloween. and as G4 said there is also roleplaying involved

In fancy dress, you buy an outfit and you wear it. In cosplay, as I understand it, there's an emphasis on skill. It's encouraged that you learn to create your own outfits, your own cosplay, instead of buying an outfit of (whatever character) from the internet or wherever you'd get it. Additionally, depending on location, it may also be encouraged to get into character, and behave as the character you're dressed as. From what I know, you'll see that type most likely at anime conventions.

So, basically, fancy dress is buying an outfit to wear. Cosplay is more related to creating the outfits, and sometimes behaving as the character instead of just dressing like them.

So how do things like people dressing up as say historical figures fit in? My mum used to make a lot of our fancy dress outfits when we were kids. I remember my mum once copied a portrait of a 16th century countess for me once (because I was a little history geek) using scraps and dresses from the charity shop and it was so good it got in the local paper. What would that be? I sort of understand it in an anime context but I've literally heard it used for things I would consider to just be fancy dress. Are those people just using the word wrong, like how people who don't understand the internet have misappropriated "troll"?

I''m not certain. I know that recently the use of the term cosplay has broadened out a bit. It's typically used to describe dressing up as characters from anime or video games, but I don't think the definition of the term itself is exclusive to those. Though unusual, I don't think it would necessarily be incorrect to use word when talking about things like historical characters. It depends on how far it's taken, like, again, whether or not they get into character at all, or if they're just dressing up. I could be wrong though. It seems to be one of those terms with a slightly indefinite meaning. As I said, it's known to be changing, so I think whether or not that's considered the correct use really depends on who you ask.
In cosplay, you are becoming the character. It's more than just a costume.
